introduction.text: The Case romane del Celio are the remains of a Roman residential complex beneath the Basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Rome's Celio district. They offer a rare glimpse into the evolution of Roman domestic architecture and the early Christian transformation of urban spaces.

history.description: The earliest part of the complex dates to the year 111, consisting of a bath on the ground floor and apartments above.
In the 3rd century the two insulae were united into a single property and transformed into a luxurious domus with frescoed rooms.
In the 4th century the complex became the property of the senator Byzas, who established a Christian titulus that later passed to his son Pammachio.
During the 5th century the foundation of the upper basilica led to the partial obliteration and burial of the Roman rooms.
The Roman rooms were uncovered at the end of the 19th century by the rector of the basilica, Padre Germano di S. Stanislao, who excavated beyond the martyrium.

design.description: The original layout comprised two insulae: one with a bath and upper apartments, the other with ground‑floor shops and upper residential spaces.
The 3rd‑century unification created a single domus featuring luxuriously frescoed rooms and a courtyard that later became a nymphaeum.
Arches that now line the basilica’s Clivo di Scauro preserve traces of the original shop façades and the courtyard’s transformation.

art.description: A large fresco scene depicting marine deities in the nymphaeum.
The Aula dell'orante fresco, likely associated with Christian use of the domus.
Frescoes in the Confessio room, which housed tombs or relics of the basilica’s titular martyrs.
